clue.text: 502 shillings invested in plant covered the wound

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500

indicators.note: invested in means put inside, like money placed within something

parts.note: a reed is a tall waterside plant
the 2 with shillings gives two S's, S being the old abbreviation for a shilling

explanation.surface: A gardener's odd tale of coins tucked inside a plant used to bandage an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 502 splits as D (500) and two S's for the shillings; 'invested in' puts SS inside REED. A shilling was an old British coin, abbreviated s.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress a wound is to clean it and put on a bandage, so the verb in its past tense fits.

clue.text: Imperfection in desert

definitions.meaning: a flaw or fault in something
to abandon one's side and go over to another

explanation.surface: A flaw found out in the desert sands.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word means a flaw; as a verb it means to abandon one's country or cause for the enemy.

clue.text: Aphrodisiac — it's in the heart, rising

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters are read from bottom to top
in places the word it inside the core

parts.note: the heart of something is its core
it is simply the word it, with the 's (is) as a link

explanation.surface: A love potion's effect described as something rising in the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' supplies just the word it, the 's being a link; 'rising' turns COITRE upward, as this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, aphrodisiac describes something that arouses desire, which is what sexually stimulating means.

clue.text: Meat cutter that's fast and keen I suspect, cook finally put away

indicators.note: put away means stowed inside, so the letter goes into the jumbled letters
suspect as an adjective means dubious, signalling the letters are not to be trusted in their order
finally picks the last letter of the word cook

explanation.surface: A kitchen tool that is quick and sharp, the cook putting it away when done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suspect' rearranges the nine letters into STEAKNIFE, and 'put away' stows the K that 'finally' gives inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak knife is a serrated table blade used to cut beef and other meat.

clue.text: Point about record store

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: a dot is a small point
EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: Making a point about a record shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a warehouse or storehouse where goods are kept.

clue.text: A flipping flat-bottomed vessel?

parts.note: describes a drinking glass with a flat base, while 'flipping' points to an acrobat who somersaults

explanation.surface: Seems to be an exasperated remark about a flat boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' reads like a mild curse but is literal: an acrobat who flips is called by the same word as a flat-based glass.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a straight-sided flat-based drinking glass and an acrobat who does somersaults.

clue.text: Opera coming over in doubly twisted old maestro

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming over means placed on top of what follows

parts.note: Tosca is Puccini's opera

indicators.note: twisted means turned round, so the letters are read backwards
doubly means the word in is taken twice

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old conductor who, twisted by opera, takes it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubly' gives ININ and 'twisted' turns it to NINI; 'coming over' sets TOSCA above it in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Arturo Toscanini was the famous Italian conductor of the early twentieth century, a celebrated musical master.

clue.text: Time in West China

indicators.note: in places one letter inside the name

parts.note: Mae West was the American film actress

explanation.surface: A time zone in western China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West' is Mae West, not a direction. 'China' means friend through Cockney rhyming slang: china plate rhymes with mate.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang china plate means pal, so china alone is a friend.

clue.text: Retro lighter in the toilet resembling member

parts.note: lav is short for lavatory
a la means in the style of
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: An old cigarette lighter found in the loo looking like a body part.
explanation.walkthrough: A LA (French, in the manner of) gives resembling.
explanation.definitionFit: The lava lamp, with its rising blobs of wax, is a 1960s light now seen as kitsch nostalgia.

clue.text: Currently in office, office in further test

indicators.note: in places the second word inside the first

parts.note: a resit is a repeat exam
a den is a private study or workroom

explanation.surface: An official currently in post must take a further test in the office.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident is someone living or working in a place now, as in a resident doctor on duty.

clue.text: West Country town mine, its gold going west?

indicators.note: in an across clue going west means running right to left, so the gold letters are turned round

parts.note: mine in the sense of meant for me, as in 'that one is for me'
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A mining town in the West Country whose gold has gone westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' is read as 'for me', not a pit; 'going west' turns the gold letters to RO in this across clue. Frome is a market town in Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: Frome is a town in Somerset, part of the south-western region called the West Country.

clue.text: River, one in West Country town — yes, yes, yes!

parts.note: the Po is Italy's longest river

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the town

parts.note: St Ives is a seaside town in Cornwall
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An ecstatic tourist's reaction to a river in a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: ST IVES is a Cornish fishing and arts town.
explanation.definitionFit: Each yes is an affirmative, so three of them are affirmatives in the plural.

clue.text: Hitter, jumper and flier

parts.note: a cricket is a leaping insect
a bat is a flying mammal

explanation.surface: A list of a sweater, a boxer and a pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' wants to be a British sweater, but here it is a leaping insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman strikes the ball with this willow blade, so it is the thing that hits.

clue.text: Policeman left inside whales

indicators.note: inside places the letter within the group word

parts.note: a pod is a group of whales

explanation.surface: A policeman abandoned inside a school of whales.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Plod is the policeman in the British children's Noddy books, so the name is slang for a plodding officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plod is British slang for a police officer, from Mr Plod in Enid Blyton's Noddy stories.

clue.text: In some parts of the plant, little troublemaker initially uses insincere praise

indicators.note: In at the start says the next pieces go within the plant parts

parts.note: stalks are stems of a plant
wee is Scottish for little

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the word troublemaker

explanation.surface: A small troublemaker in the garden flatters people with false praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' leads the clue but governs everything after it: WEET goes into the stems just after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweet-talk someone is to coax them with flattery, so the third-person verb means flatters.

clue.text: See 22
Beneath top of mainmast, cast-iron case for the quarterdeck, perhaps?

indicators.note: in a down clue, beneath means the following letters sit below the first one
top of takes the first letter of the word mainmast
cast means thrown into a new shape, so the letters of iron are rearranged

parts.note: a suit is a legal case

explanation.surface: Nautical instructions about a cast-iron box kept under the mast on the ship's deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' shuffles IRON into INOR. In bridge, diamonds and clubs are the minor suits, each a quarter of the pack: a 'quarter deck'.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit is one quarter of a deck of cards, and diamonds or clubs are the minor ones in bridge.

clue.text: Something dynamic, perhaps, in horribly dire wet bottom?

indicators.note: in puts the word for something dynamic inside the jumbled letters
horribly suggests something badly mangled, so the letters of dire are rearranged

parts.note: a dynamic verb, describing action, is one kind of verb

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about something energetic down in a dreadfully damp bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horribly' makes RIED from the fodder. Grammar calls action words like run dynamic verbs, so 'something dynamic, perhaps' is a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The floor of a river channel is the ground lying always underwater, a literally soaked base.

clue.text: Moving out of Paignton?

indicators.note: out of here means formed from the letters of, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone leaving a Devon seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' looks like the act of relocating, but it is the definition in the sense of touching. PAIGNTON is a seaside resort in Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: Something poignant stirs the emotions, just as a moving story touches the heart.

clue.text: Harmless drunk missing wife, figure touring the bogs

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: a wino is a habitual drunk

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so the number goes around the marshes

parts.note: five is a number, a figure
fens are marshy lowlands

explanation.surface: A drunk without his wife staggers round the marshes, doing no harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' leaves INO; 'touring' gives FFENSIVE. 'Bogs' looks like British slang for toilets but means marshes here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inoffensive causes no upset or injury to anyone, so it is benign.

clue.text: Street, then turn for promenade

parts.note: a roll is a turning motion

explanation.surface: Directions: go down the street and then turn for the seafront.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promenade' looks like a seaside walkway noun, but it is the verb-or-noun for a leisurely walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A promenade is a leisurely walk taken for pleasure, the same as an amble or saunter.

clue.text: Mythical flier, wacky with vulture and raven wings

indicators.note: the wings of each word are its outermost letters, first and last

explanation.surface: A crazy flying monster made of vulture and raven wings.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a heraldic two-legged winged dragon, a legendary creature of the air.

clue.text: Advantage held by landed gentry

indicators.note: held by means contained within, so the letters are found inside the phrase

explanation.surface: The landowning classes keep their privileges.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the edge over a rival means having a slight superiority over them.

clue.text: Words from Hamlet confusing family with satyr in the West Country

indicators.note: confusing means mixing up, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: Oman is a country in the Middle East

explanation.surface: A garbled line from Shakespeare about a mixed-up family and a mythical goat-man in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the West Country' wants to be one place name; instead IN THE joins the anagram, West is W and Country is OMAN. Hamlet himself compares his uncle to a satyr.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet says this line in his first soliloquy, condemning his mother for remarrying so quickly.

clue.text: Byzantine empress turning up in Tenerife

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means read from the bottom upwards
in means the letters are found inside the word

explanation.surface: An empress from Byzantium appearing on a Canary Island holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' picks ENERI out of Tenerife, and 'turning up' turns it the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene of Athens ruled the Byzantine Empire as sole sovereign at the end of the eighth century.

clue.text: Not entirely green, a South American capital

indicators.note: not entirely means one letter short of the full word, so its end is cut

parts.note: lime is a shade of green

explanation.surface: A city described as not completely green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' drops the last letter of LIME, leaving LIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Lima is the capital city of Peru, on the Pacific coast of the continent.

clue.text: Cryptically, what might one do with a Cornish pasty and where? That's bliss!

indicators.note: cryptically warns the pieces combine unusually, the eating set within the place

parts.note: Bude is a Cornish seaside town, a place a pasty might be eaten

parts.words: what might one do with a Cornish pasty
parts.note: with a pasty, one would eat it

explanation.surface: A riddle about enjoying a Cornish pasty, and where, ending in blissful contentment.
explanation.walkthrough: EAT IT goes inside BUDE, a seaside town in Cornwall. A Cornish pasty is a folded pastry filled with meat and vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: A beatitude is a state of supreme blessedness, as in the blessings Jesus gave in the Sermon on the Mount.

clue.text: Abandoned ship's first to enter West Country town

indicators.note: to enter means to go into, so the letter is placed inside the town

parts.note: Looe is a small fishing town in Cornwall

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the word ship

explanation.surface: An abandoned ship's captain is the first to come into a Cornish harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' gives S from ship's, and 'to enter' puts it inside LOOE, a Cornish fishing port.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose here means unrestrained or wanton, as in loose living, an abandoned way of behaving.

clue.text: Draw away from Land's End, England trailing rapidly away, Cornwall too, for starters

indicators.note: End here means the last letter of the word Land
for starters means the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Instructions for a quick escape from Cornwall's tip, England falling away fast behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Land's End is the far western tip of Cornwall, but here 'End' just takes D from Land.
explanation.definitionFit: To detract from something is to reduce or take away from its worth.

clue.text: Greek character taking drug with the ability to say "sausages" backwards?

parts.note: E is short for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: backwards means read in reverse order

parts.note: someone with no lisp can pronounce sibilant words like sausages cleanly

explanation.surface: A Greek person on drugs claiming they can pronounce a tricky word in reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backwards' looks attached to saying the word, but it turns NO LISP into PSILON.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth letter of the Greek alphabet.
